en: Candrāvalokana. The preceding text is the *Amaraughaprabodha* in 74 verses; the *Candrāvalokana* begins on the recto.
Note: Collate the readings from MGOL 4344 as provided in the catalogue; scan into the CA folder.
MGOL D-4345, folios 46r–48v:
Oṃ. Maheśvara said:
"The internal object of focus, with the gaze directed outward, free from the opening and closing of the eyes—"
This is that Śāmbhavī Mudrā, hidden in all tantras:
when the yogin exists with his mind and breath focused on the internal object,
looking outward with an unwavering gaze, he should always see neither the lower nor the higher.
This indeed is the Khecarī Mudrā, which arises through the grace of the Guru—
the reality that shines forth, free from both void and non-void, the state of Śambhu.
With half-opened eyes, with a steady mind, and with the gaze fixed on the tip of the nose...

When the moon and the sun have entered into dissolution, one attains that supreme state, the highest reality which is motionless in form, luminous in nature, devoid of all externality, and intensely radiant;
what more need be said here regarding that which is the ultimate object of expression?
That dissolution which is experienced within when one is situated in the womb and perceives the internal dissolution—
that too should be understood as being accompanied by a satisfied Guru.
That consciousness of all beings is the witness of their arising and passing away.
Behold that consciousness, established within the body, which is the nectar abiding in the bliss of the vital breaths.
Where Śiva is in one place, the mind in another, and the power (Śakti) in another from the Mother,
the supreme ascent is not accomplished even in hundreds of millions of aeons.
Whence can there be knowledge while the mind lives as long as false views persist?
Even the vital breath lives only so long as the mind does not die;
when both this vital breath and the mind reach dissolution—
That man goes to liberation; no other does so in any way.
He who, regarding unions and separations, [perceives] neither pleasure nor the like, and whose view is not fixed upon the objects of the senses, is not bound by the net of existence.
Where there is vision, there is the mind, and there the eternal elements and senses reside;
that is the power of all beings, the vision having merged into the object of perception.
Where there is vision, there is stability of mind, and therein indeed [arises] from ego-sense (abhimāna).
If it were thus for you, then that which is established and accepted by us would be proven for you as well:
(10) "The form of an unbroken circle, existing both externally and internally, is seen even at the tip of the eye; yet one does not see it with the eye alone. (11)

Just as a gem that is constantly shimmering, situated at the tip of the eye, does not perceive itself even when seen, so too the light of the self (*ātman*), the light of the mind (*manas*), and the light of the eye do not see one another.
12. Even having seen that which causes attainment, one is liberated from bonds.
The light of the mantra, the light of the mind, the light, and the eye do not see [one another].
The light that is both external and internal to Śiva— that light is called Śiva.
As long as the moving vital breath does not enter the central path,
and as long as the flow of the vital wind is not firmly established as the *bindu*, [so long is he not Śiva].

As long as [the mind] is not born equal and serene, and as long as there is no state of non-arrogance—if one speaks of obstacles, deceit, and false prattle—[that is the sign]. 14 = HP 4.114 (end of folio;
beginning of 47r).

Someone who is constantly devoted to practice and always devoted to the guru, yet does not know the innate [nature], proceeds like an egg. The new moon (*āmāvāsya*), the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), and the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) are concealed. (cf. below)

Desire is indeed poison from the stainless [state]... served everywhere. 16. Those who are filled with passion at the outset—who among them acts like a Brahmin? 17. Deceived by false pride, they do not know things as they truly are.
The new moon, the first day of the lunar fortnight, and the full moon are concealed.
At will, the stainless poison stands above all.
Matsyendra said:
"O Śaṅkara, how is that designation [of time] truly explained by all its definitions on the new moon (āmāvāsyā), the first day (pratipad), and the full moon (paurṇamāsī)? Īśvara said:
Matsyendra says that the new moon (*āmāvāsyā*) is the opening of the eye of the Path (*pratipat*), while the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) is the half-glance of the Three-Eyed One (*Trilocanā*). 20.
Matsyendra.
If it is desire, what more need be said? Or if it is poison, what is being expressed?
Tell me truly, who is this whose nature is stainless? 21. Īśvara.

The *pratipad* swallows time, and likewise the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). [The path] becomes manifest; it is not otherwise. Through desire comes the longing for sense objects; from poison comes the dissolution of that desire.

One should abandon these two [damaged], and take refuge in the stainless. (YKU 3.3) Another should renounce everything if he desires his own welfare; otherwise, there is indeed death, for [the fruits] have already been consumed. (YKU 4ab)
Having placed the mind in the midst of the *śakti*, and having [placed] the mind within the midst of the *śakti*,
one should perceive the mind with the mind and meditate upon that supreme state—
thus says Matsyendra.
What is the bindu called? What is the characteristic of the bindu like?
And how does the bindu arise? Explain this according to reality. —Īśvara.
The mind alone is indeed the drop (*bindu*), the cause of both arising and abiding. From the mind the drop arises, just as milk [is the cause] of that which consists of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
— Matsyendra.
Pervading from the crown of the head to the tips of the nails, that which is both pleasure and pain dissolves;
what kind of bondage can there be for it within the cavity of the bell?
—The Lord.

Neither one situated within the bonds, nor one whose mind is fixed on a single object; having known the Śakti located above the moon, wherever she resides, there the bondage is [found]. Having understood this, one should pierce the Suṣumnā and cause the vital breath (vāyu) to enter the center.
Having performed [this] in the place of the *bindu*, one should restrain it within the nasal cavity.
Matsyendra has declared that the wind (*vāyu*), the *bindu*, and likewise the principle (*tattva*) and primordial nature (*prakṛti*), are all one.
"I do not know the six wheels; please be gracious and tell them to me.
Īśvara replied: "The Ādhāra, the Svādhiṣṭhāna, and the Maṇipūra as the third."

The unstruck (*anāhata*) and the pure (*viśuddha*), and the sixth is the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*). The foundation (*ādhāra*) is said to be the anus, and the self-sustained (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is the genital organ. The jewel-filling (*maṇipūra*) is in the region of the navel, and the unstruck (*anāhata*) resides in the heart.
The pure [cakra] is in the region of the throat, and the *ājñā*-cakra is at the crown of the head. Having fully understood these six cakras, one should enter the *dhruvamaṇḍala*.
One should enter by drawing in the breath and likewise direct it upward.
One should practice in this manner until one becomes identical with the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).
One should practice the unification of the vital air (vāyu), the drop (bindu), and the wheel (cakra) within the mind.
Through this, yogis attain immortality simultaneously with samādhi.

Just as fire situated within wood does not arise without friction, so too the radiance of knowledge does not indeed manifest without the yoga of practice. Just as a lamp inside a jar does not illuminate the exterior, [so it is with knowledge].

Just as the flame of a lamp shines within a broken jar, so too is the jar said to be one's own nature; for that very word "lamp" is indeed the state [of liberation]. Through the Guru’s words, when [the jar] is broken, the knowledge of Brahman becomes manifest.
Having obtained a Guru who acts as a helmsman and having practiced the subtle [path], they cross over;
those empowered by the latent impressions of practice cross the ocean of existence.
Matsyendra said:
"By your grace alone, O Lord of the gods, I am liberated from the bonds of existence;
you are my refuge, O Śaṅkara, there is no other for me.
Having heard the words of Matsyendra, the Blessed Lord Śiva was delighted and entered [the state of grace].
"O Gaṅgāputra, you shall be renowned and you shall uplift the three worlds.
Thus ends the *Candrāvalokana* composed by Maheśvara. Homage to the illustrious Guru-nātha. (The text consists of 42 verses.)
